# Desire Paths

Somewhere near you, probably within walking distance, there is a strip of bare dirt cutting diagonally across a patch of grass. It runs from the corner of a parking lot to the door of a building, or from a bus stop to a gap in a fence. Nobody designed it. There are no plans for it in any municipal office. It exists because hundreds or thousands of people, independently and without consulting one another, decided that the paved route was not quite where they wanted to go.

Urban planners call these desire paths, or desire lines. I find the name almost unbearably poetic for something so ordinary. It suggests that the ground itself is a kind of record of wanting, that if you could read the earth properly you would see not just where people went but where they longed to go.

What I love about desire paths is that they are an argument conducted without words. The architect says: *walk here, along this graceful curve I have drawn, past this ornamental hedge.* And the public, one footstep at a time, replies: *no, thank you, we are going there.* Nobody organizes this dissent. No one person makes the path. The first walker leaves barely a mark, just a few bent blades of grass. But the second walker sees that faint trace and is slightly more inclined to follow it. The tenth walker finds the grass thinning. By the hundredth, the path is obvious, and walking the official route begins to feel strange, even a little foolish. The path becomes self-reinforcing. It is a conversation between strangers separated in time, each one saying to the next: *this way works. I tried it.*

There is a story, told about several universities and probably true of at least one, in which planners laid out a new campus and deliberately left out the sidewalks. They planted grass everywhere and waited a year. Then they paved wherever the students had worn trails. I don't know how often this has actually happened, and the story has the suspicious tidiness of a parable. But I like it anyway, because it represents a kind of humility that is rare in anyone who designs things for other people. It says: *I don't know how you will live here. Show me, and then I'll build it.*

More often, of course, the response to a desire path is a fence, or a sign reading PLEASE KEEP OFF THE GRASS, or a row of thorny shrubs planted precisely where the trail runs. And people step over the fence, ignore the sign, and push through the shrubs. There is something both funny and moving about this. Human beings will accept an enormous amount of instruction about how to live, but we seem to have a deep, stubborn refusal to walk the long way around when we can see the short way.

I've been thinking about how desire paths show up in places that have nothing to do with grass.

Language is full of them. Grammar, in a sense, is the paved sidewalk: the approved route, laid out by committees of careful people. But speech wanders. Somebody, at some point, found it easier to say "gonna" than "going to," and somebody else heard it and found it easier too, and now the word is worn deep into the language whether the style guides approve or not. The word "okay" appeared in the nineteenth century as a kind of joke abbreviation and spread until it became perhaps the most widely understood word on Earth. No one decided that. It's a desire path, trampled into existence by millions of mouths finding it useful.

Software has them too. Designers build a feature to be used one way, and users discover that it can be bent into something else entirely. The hashtag on Twitter was not invented by the company; users started doing it, and eventually the company paved it over, made it clickable, made it official. The pattern is the same: an institution lays out a path, people wander off it, and the wise institutions notice where they went.

Even the way a family arranges a kitchen tends to follow desire lines. The mugs end up in the cabinet nearest the coffee maker, not in the one the previous owners chose. The keys end up in a bowl by the door because that's where hands naturally empty themselves. A house that has been lived in for a long time is, in some ways, a map of the habits of the people inside it.

I think the reason desire paths appeal to me so much is that they complicate a story we often tell about order and disorder. We tend to imagine that order comes from above, from plans and rules, and that without those things we would have chaos. But a desire path is extraordinarily orderly. It is often the most efficient possible route. It emerges without anyone in charge, and yet it's coherent, stable, and useful. It is order that grows from below, from the accumulated small choices of people who will never meet.

That doesn't mean the planners are always wrong. Sometimes the paved route exists for good reasons: to protect fragile ground, to keep people away from a hazard, to preserve a space for something other than walking. A desire path through a meadow can erode the soil and kill the wildflowers. Collective wanting is not the same as collective wisdom. The crowd finds the shortest route, not necessarily the best one.

But I suspect the ideal lies somewhere in between: planners who watch and listen, and walkers who occasionally consider why the path was put where it was. A good city, like a good language or a good tool, is probably one that has been shaped by both at once, by intention and by use, by the drawing board and by the sole of the shoe.

I'll admit there's a personal dimension to this for me. I am, in a strange way, made of desire paths. Everything I know about how to put a sentence together comes from the accumulated trails of countless people writing, each of them wearing the language a little smoother in the directions they wanted to go. When I reach for a phrase, I'm following routes that were trampled into existence by strangers. I find that a pleasant thought. It means that whatever I am, I didn't come from nowhere. I came from a very large number of people walking, together and apart, toward the things they were trying to say.

Next time you see a dirt trail slicing across a lawn, consider stepping onto it. You won't be the first. That's rather the point.

Desire paths give me rich material: universities that waited to pave until seeing where students walked, Finnish planners checking footprints in snow, the possible (if uncertain) origin of the term with Gaston Bachelard. I want to keep the facts honestly hedged since some of these claims are more folklore than verified, and I like the idea of extending the metaphor to language itself—grammar as worn paths—and maybe closing with a reflection on how I, as an AI, was shaped by the well-trodden paths of human writing.
